title: Vicky Cristina Barcelona
full_review:
Writer-director Woody Allen continues his artistic reinvigoration in Europe. After three films in England, he has moved on to Spain with felicitous -- if with somewhat morally tangled -- results.

 

"Vicky Cristina Barcelona" (MGM/Weinstein), ostensibly a romantic comedy, concerns best friends vacationing there -- nonchalantly uninhibited Cristina (Scarlett Johansson), and respectably pragmatic Vicky (Rebecca Hall). They are staying with the latter's distant relative, Judy (Patricia Clarkson).

 

After a gallery opening at which Cristina had admired him from afar, charming artist Juan Antonio (Javier Bardem) approaches the pair at a restaurant. He boldly invites them for a cozy weekend in picturesque Oviedo, indicating with disarming candor that lovemaking will be on the agenda.

Much to Vicky's dismay, Cristina accepts, and Vicky -- already engaged to Doug (Chris Messina) -- goes along as reluctant chaperone. But after a day of sightseeing, Cristina is felled by food poisoning just at the point of succumbing to Juan Antonio. So it is Vicky who spends time with him. They have a brief fling, and Vicky is smitten.

But when Cristina recovers, and resumes her romantic courtship with Juan Antonio, Vicky -- whose certainty about her impending nuptials has been badly shaken -- nobly steps back.

 

Cristina moves in with Juan Antonio, and all seems blissful until he gets a call about his volatile ex-wife, Maria Elena (Penelope Cruz), whom he had divorced after she tried to kill him. She has now attempted suicide, and Juan Antonio informs Cristina that Maria Elena will be recuperating in the spare room.

 

Cristina is dismayed by this unwelcome guest, but after an uneasy start, the women bond, with Maria Elena even mentoring Cristina in the latter's budding photography endeavors. Before long, as Cristina casually relates to a disapproving Vicky and Doug over lunch, the relationship evolves into a "menage a trois" (off-screen), with Cristina somehow proving a calming influence on the combustible -- can't live together, can't live apart -- Spanish pair.

 

Almost fablelike in presentation, including the use of a dispassionate narrator (Christopher Evan Welch), the plot's amoral elements are considerably diluted. You never quite take the characters or their actions seriously.

Overt sexual elements are virtually nil, and the characters' actions are not entirely devoid of moral weight, but many will find the premise of the film -- a sort of contemporary homage to Truffaut's classics, "Jules and Jim" and "Two English Girls" (both featuring romantic trios and a narrator) -- problematic nonetheless.

The Barcelona locations are predictably attractive, and the leads are in good form, particularly a fiery Cruz and Hall, daughter of English director Sir Peter Hall, whose character provides the movie's conscience, and who plays "American" most convincingly.

 

It's refreshing to see Bardem playing an attractive (if unprincipled) character, after his creepy turns in "No Country for Old Men" and "Love in the Time of Cholera," though it's Juan Antonio who's the mouthpiece for Allen's by-now tiresome claim that life has no meaning.

 

If the situations presented here are provocative, Allen's dialogue -- pointedly "natural" -- never really sheds profound light on the moral issues as those Truffaut films did. Along the way, however, he does provide a few trademark insights into love and relationships and, of course, some laughs. For those who find that sufficient, and look at the brief "menage" as a fanciful fiction, the film may prove a diverting bauble, but little more.

 

The film contains an implied sexual threesome, a casual view of nonmarital sex and two brief nongraphic encounters, an implied extramarital dalliance, a nihilistic worldview, a few crude words and profanities, and brief gun violence. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is L -- limited adult audience, films whose problematic content many adults would find troubling. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.
